title: FRM Operational, Lesson 13: Operational risk capital and the standardised measurement approach
subtitle: Why Basel abandoned internal models and went back to one standard formula for everyone
whyItMatters: Operational risk was once allowed to be capitalised with internal models, and then Basel withdrew that permission entirely. Understanding why is a large lesson about the limits of quantitative modelling when the data is too sparse and the person doing the calculation has an incentive for the number to come out small.
openingQuestion: Why did Basel III withdraw the advanced measurement approach based on internal models for operational risk?
openingOptions: Because capital differed too much between banks with similar risk profiles
Because internal models always produced far more capital than was actually needed
Because banks lacked the technological capacity to run internal models properly
Because operational risk stopped being treated as a risk type requiring capital
explanation: The Basel Committee's review found that two banks with near-identical risk profiles were arriving at very different capital numbers, mostly because of technical choices inside the model. With sparse tail data and a modeller who has an incentive to reduce capital, modelling freedom becomes a problem rather than a virtue.

diagram.label: Business indicator component: the scale of activity from the financial statements
Multiplied by a marginal coefficient that rises with size
Multiplied by the internal loss multiplier from ten years of loss history
Out comes required capital - comparable across banks

realWorldExample.company: The trade-off between risk sensitivity and comparability
realWorldExample.description: Replacing internal models with a standard formula is the clearest example of the central trade-off in all capital regulation: the more sensitive a model is to an institution's own risk profile, the harder it is to compare across institutions and the easier it is to optimise in the modeller's favour. Basel accepted a loss of sensitivity in exchange for comparability and resistance to manipulation.

quiz.question: What quantity does the business indicator component in the SMA rest on?
options: The total count of operational risk events recorded in the past year
The number of staff and the number of branches the bank operates
The market value of shareholders' equity at the end of the year
Income and expense lines taken from the financial statements
quiz.explanation: The underlying assumption is that the larger a bank's activity, the larger its exposure to operational risk. Using audited financial statement figures makes the input far harder to manipulate than an internal model parameter. An event count would reward under-reporting, headcount and branch numbers describe an operating model rather than a scale of activity, and equity market value moves with sentiment rather than with operational exposure.

quiz.question: What does the internal loss multiplier bring into the SMA formula?
options: The bank's own realised loss history
The average rate of inflation in the country
A credit rating from an international agency
The number of financial products the bank sells
quiz.explanation: If capital depended on size alone, a bank with strong controls and a bank that keeps suffering losses would carry the same requirement, leaving no incentive to improve. This multiplier retains a degree of risk sensitivity inside a standard formula. Inflation and credit ratings describe the environment rather than operational performance, and a product count is a business-mix statistic that says nothing about control quality.

quiz.question: Why is capital not the primary tool for managing operational risk?
options: Because regulation imposes no requirement to hold any capital
Because capital only absorbs losses after they have occurred
Because losses are never large enough to require capital
Because capital is refunded at the end of the financial year
quiz.explanation: Capital is a cushion that absorbs consequences, not a preventive measure. A bank with enough capital for a major fraud still loses the money and still loses reputation - closing the control gap is what stops the loss arising in the first place. Regulation does require operational risk capital, operational losses have repeatedly run into billions, and capital is not returned at year end but held permanently against the exposure.

quiz.question: Why did Basel move from internal models to a standardised approach for operational risk?
options: Because operational loss data may no longer be used in capital calculations
Because the internal model approach always gave less capital than needed
Because two banks with similar risk profiles arrived at very different capital
Because smaller banks lacked the resources to build an internal model at all
quiz.explanation: With extremely sparse tail data and a modeller who has an incentive to reduce capital, modelling freedom became a stronger driver of the result than the underlying risk profile. Standardisation trades sensitivity for comparability across institutions. Loss data is still used, through the internal loss multiplier, the bias was not uniformly downward across banks, and resource constraints at small banks were handled by simply not requiring them to model.

quiz.question: What role does operational risk capital play in the risk management framework?
options: An indicator reflecting the quality of the internal control system
The main tool for cutting the frequency and severity of incidents
A provision set aside to cover fines imposed by the supervisor
A loss-absorbing layer, not a tool for making incidents less likely
quiz.explanation: Capital prevents no incident whatsoever - it only ensures the institution survives one. What genuinely reduces risk is process, control points and culture; capital is the last layer after all three have failed. It is not a quality indicator either, because it is driven mostly by the scale of the business, and it is not a provision earmarked against any particular category of loss such as regulatory fines.

practicePrompt.question: A bank has a clean operational loss history, so its internal loss multiplier is low and required capital comes down. Management treats this as evidence that risk is well managed. Which statement is correct?
options: Low capital is a result, not a tool for reducing risk
Correct, since the SMA formula already reflects control quality
Wrong, because the loss multiplier has nothing to do with controls
Correct, provided the loss data was fully audited
practicePrompt.explanation: The internal loss multiplier does indeed bring the bank's own loss history into the formula, so low capital does reflect a clean past. But capital works in the opposite direction to what management is assuming: it ABSORBS the consequences after an event, it does not make the event less likely. What genuinely reduces risk is control - segregation of duties, independent reconciliation, new product approval - and no amount of capital substitutes for them. A clean history is also a small sample from a very fat-tailed distribution: it says the bank has not yet met a large event, not that it will not.

keyTakeaways: Basel dropped internal models for operational risk because results lacked comparability and were easy to adjust
The SMA rests on a business indicator component taken from audited financial statements
The internal loss multiplier keeps some sensitivity to each bank's own control quality
Capital absorbs consequences; controls are what actually reduce risk

summary.keyIdea: Moving from internal models to a standard formula trades risk sensitivity for comparability and resistance to manipulation
summary.commonMistake: Reading the operational risk capital number as a measure of risk management quality, when it mostly reflects the scale of the business
summary.action: When assessing an institution's operational risk management, look at the loss data and the control system before you look at the capital number

application.title: Reading a bank's capital disclosure
application.message: In a bank's annual report, find the operational risk capital section and compare its weight against credit risk capital - the difference tells you something about the shape of their business model.
application.secondary: A bank tilted towards services and payments usually carries a higher operational risk share than one tilted towards lending.

sections.text: Operational risk is the only risk type Basel ever permitted internal models for and then withdrew entirely - and the reason for the withdrawal is more instructive than the replacement formula itself.

Three factors combined: tail data so sparse that the choice of distribution dominated the result; several equally defensible technical choices producing capital numbers far apart from one another; and a modeller with a clear incentive for the number to be small. The consequence was two similar banks arriving at two capital levels that could not be compared.

The formula starts from the scale of activity through a business indicator component built from financial statement line items, multiplies it by a marginal coefficient that rises in size bands, then adjusts it with an internal loss multiplier computed from that bank's own realised loss history over many years.

sections.label: The central trade-off in capital regulation
sections.text: The more sensitive to an institution's specifics, the harder to compare across institutions and the easier to optimise in the modeller's favour. The more standardised, the easier to compare but the less it reflects real risk. There is no absolutely right answer, only a choice about which way to lean.
Why internal models failed for this particular risk type

Three factors combined. First, tail data is extremely sparse: a bank may never have suffered a billion-dollar loss event, so the choice of distributional form - not the data - decides most of the capital number. Second, there are too many equally defensible modelling choices producing results that differ by multiples. Third, the consequence of the first two: two banks with almost identical risk profiles still published very different capital levels, and nobody could say which one was right.

sections.label: What the standardised approach buys instead
sections.text: The formula starts from the scale of activity, built from line items already present in the financial statements, with a marginal coefficient that rises with size - a larger bank must hold more capital per unit of revenue. It is then adjusted by the institution's own realised loss history, averaged over ten years so that one unusual year cannot dominate the result. The structure deliberately puts comparability ahead of sensitivity to each institution's specifics - a conscious choice, not a lazy simplification.

left.label: More sensitive to each institution's specifics
left.text: The capital number reflects one particular bank's real risk profile more faithfully. But it is hard to compare across institutions, and every degree of freedom in the model is a place where the result can be optimised in your own favour.

right.label: More standardised
right.text: Comparable and hard to distort, but it does not reward a bank with a better control system. That is the central trade-off in all capital regulation, and for operational risk Basel chose firmly in favour of standardisation after trying the other side.

lines: Capital is a cushion, not a fence; the fence is the control system.
Next lesson: the risk group whose penalties have grown fastest - conduct and compliance risk.
